chunks: "The common-mode voltage is the average of the two wires of a differential pair, V-plus plus V-minus over two. It's what's left when you remove the signal.

If I write each wire as the common-mode level plus or minus half the differential voltage, then the signal is the part that's opposite on the two wires and the common-mode is the part that's the same.
In a clean link it's a fixed DC offset set by the driver, for example 1. 2 volts for LVDS, around 2. 5 volts for CAN, and whatever the bias network sets for an AC-coupled link.
In a real system it also carries noise and ground offset, which is what the receiver is meant to reject. It matters in three ways.
First, the receiver has a common-mode input range.
If a ground offset or a bad bias pushes the average outside it, the input stage saturates and the link fails even though the differential signal is fine.
Second, how much it leaks into the output is set by the CMRR.
Third, a common-mode current on a cable is a very efficient antenna, so a noisy or unbalanced common-mode shows up as an EMI problem.
To measure it, I'd probe both wires single-ended against ground and use the scope math function, channel one plus channel two divided by two."
